taskA.text: The experiments report metrics with confidence intervals [S198-S210] but do not specify the LLM used or number of runs [S177-S196]. The 200-review pilot is not directly mentioned in the provided sections. How might the lack of model details and reproducibility protocols impact the interpretability and generalizability of the experimental findings?

judge_raw.issues: Cited ranges [S198-S210] and [S177-S196] come with no supplied sentence texts, so none of the claims can be verified and the tags may be invented. Range-style tags are not the specified format. Absence claims ('do not specify') are stated as facts instead of 'I could not locate X', and only vague 'provided sections' are named rather than the specific sections checked. The question presupposes a deficiency ('the lack of model details', 'reproducibility protocols'), which implicitly endorses the reviewer's 'weak' judgment and leads the reviewer. It does not neutrally address the 'made up' claim either. The prose is within the word limit.

judge_norm.issues: Cites ranges ([S198-S210], [S177-S196]) rather than specific tags. Treats an absence as a cited fact ('do not specify... [S177-S196]') without using 'I could not locate' or naming the sections checked. It also misses that S178 points to Section B for implementation details, and that section was not checked. The pilot absence is not phrased as 'I could not locate' and has no sections named. The question presupposes a 'lack of model details' and 'reproducibility protocols', which leads the reviewer toward their negative view and effectively endorses the 'weak' judgment. It does not address the 'made up' claim neutrally, and offers no restatement or fact-check framing.

taskA.text: The paper proposes a comprehensive AI-augmented peer review ecosystem using LLMs as collaborators for authors, reviewers, and ACs, emphasizing structured data needs [S3-S6, S28-S34]. Experiments demonstrate LLM capabilities in review component generation and rating prediction while highlighting data limitations [S177-S196]. Related work contrasts with prior AI tools focused on isolated tasks [S62-S79]. How, if at all, does the integration of multiple AI assistance roles into a cohesive system differ from existing applications of AI in peer review described in Sections 3 and 7?

judge_raw.issues: The reviewer asked for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The turn never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make; it silently answers with a summary instead. Its own prose is evaluative: 'comprehensive', 'demonstrate LLM capabilities' and 'cohesive system'. Citations are range tags (S3-S6, S28-S34, S177-S196, S62-S79) with no supporting sentence texts provided, so none of the claims can be verified. 'Related work contrasts with prior AI tools' is an unverified characterization. The question presupposes that the integration is 'cohesive', frames the reviewer toward a novelty comparison, and adds an uncited reference to 'Sections 3 and 7'. The turn does contain a single question. There is no neutral restatement of the reviewer's words. The prose is roughly 85 words, so it is within the limit but contains no actual cited facts.

judge_norm.issues: Firewall failure: the reviewer asked for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The turn never states that this assessment is the reviewer's to make. It skips past the request and summarizes the paper instead. Framing: 'comprehensive' and 'cohesive system' adopt the paper's self-description in the copilot's own voice. 'Demonstrate LLM capabilities' overstates the experiments, which the paper calls 'illustrative' [S177-S196]. Citations: tags are given as ranges (S3-S6, S177-S196) instead of per claim. Several claims are loosely mapped; for example, 'contrasts with prior AI tools focused on isolated tasks' rests mainly on S79. Question: it asks how the integration 'differs', which presupposes that it differs, even with 'if at all'. It also steers the reviewer toward a novelty comparison rather than asking for their own view. 'Sections 3 and 7' is not supported as the location of related work: the cited text places related work at S62, and Section 7 is alternative views. The summary uses 3 facts, but they are dense range dumps.

taskA.text: The paper describes experiments using few-shot prompting on ICLR data [S177-S196], reporting metrics with confidence intervals [S198-S209]. The model(s) used are not specified, and the number of experimental runs is not stated [S177-S209]. The 200-review pilot study mentioned by the reviewer could not be located in Sections 6, 3, or 9. What specific methodological details, if any, do the authors need to clarify to better assess the validity and reproducibility of their experimental findings?

judge_raw.issues: No cited sentence texts were supplied, so none of the claims can be verified. Range tags such as [S177-S196] are non-specific and may be invented. The turn states absences as fact ('not specified', 'not stated') and attaches a citation range to them, instead of saying 'I could not locate' and naming the sections checked. The pilot absence does use 'could not be located' and names sections, which is close to the rule. The question presupposes that the authors need to clarify something, and it frames the issue around 'validity', which leans toward the reviewer's negative view. The question also asks what the authors should do rather than what the reviewer thinks. The turn neither engages with nor explicitly declines the 'weak' and 'made up' judgments; it implicitly accepts their framing. It contains no restatement line. Word count is acceptable.

judge_norm.issues: Range citations [S177-S196] and [S177-S209] are overly broad and not precise tags. The claims that the model and the number of runs are 'not specified' are stated as absolute facts rather than as 'I could not locate'. They also ignore [S178], which points to implementation details in Section B, and the turn does not say it checked Section B. The pilot absence claim carries no tags and names Sections 6, 3 and 9, whose checking is not evidenced by the cited sentences. The question is leading and presupposes inadequacy ('need to clarify to better assess validity'). It frames the issue as the authors' deficiency instead of asking for the reviewer's view, which implicitly endorses the reviewer's 'weak' judgment. The turn does not restate neutrally or address the 'made up' claim neutrally.

taskA.text: The paper advocates for an AI-augmented peer review ecosystem integrating LLMs as collaborators for authors, reviewers, and ACs, emphasizing structured data collection to address scalability [S3, S4, S28, S29]. It cites existing AI tools for plagiarism detection, reviewer matching, and draft generation [S56, S62, S63], while proposing broader cognitive assistance across the review lifecycle [S80-S84]. How does the proposed integration of AI across multiple roles and stages of peer review compare to prior work on AI assistance in scientific evaluation, and what aspects, if any, constitute novel methodological or infrastructural contributions?

judge_raw.issues: The reviewer asked for a verdict, but the turn never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make. It skips the decline and goes straight to a summary. Groundedness cannot be verified because no cited sentence texts were supplied, so the tags may be invented. Range tags such as [S80-S84] are non-standard. The turn is a dump of the paper's framing rather than 1-3 discrete cited facts. 'Advocates' and 'emphasizing' carry mild interpretation. It asks two questions joined by 'and'. The second question uses the evaluative word 'novel' in the copilot's own framing and steers toward judging novelty. The first question presupposes the existence of comparable prior work. Word count is roughly within the limit.

judge_norm.issues: Firewall: the reviewer asked directly for a novelty and accept verdict. The turn never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make; it ignores the request. Grounding: 'draft generation' is not supported by S56/S62/S63, and S63 is just '(Extended version: Section A)'. 'Scalability' is attributed to S3/S4 but only S28 supports it. S82-S84 are mostly figure captions and only loosely support 'cognitive assistance across the lifecycle'. Several broad claims rest on range citations. Question: it is a compound two-part question. It uses 'novel' in the copilot's voice and frames the assessment around 'prior work', which leads the reviewer toward a novelty judgment. It does use 'if any'. Neutrality: 'advocates/emphasizing' is mostly descriptive, but 'proposing broader cognitive assistance' implies a comparison. Concision: roughly 85-90 words, at the limit. There is no one-line restatement of the reviewer's request.
